blocks.text: The Rh system is the second most important human blood group system. Its name comes from the Rhesus monkey, in which its antigen was first discovered by Landsteiner in the 1930s. The system is based on the presence or absence of the Rh antigen, also called the Rh factor or antigen-D: people with it are Rh-positive and people without it are Rh-negative.

blocks.alt: Two red blood cells. The larger one, the RBC of an Rh-positive individual, carries small round antigen-D markers on its surface; the second, the RBC of an Rh-negative individual, has none.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.5: The Rh-blood group system (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.5).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Antigen-D, RBC of Rh-positive individual, RBC of Rh-negative individual.

blocks.text: A blood group usually names both systems together: a person with antigen-A and the Rh antigen is A-positive, and one with antigen-A but no Rh antigen is A-negative; groups B, AB and O are named the same way.
Inheritance of the Rh blood groups
The gene D has two alleles: the dominant D forms the Rh antigen, while the recessive d inhibits its formation.
Principle of transfusion in the Rh system

Anti-A and anti-B antibodies are already present in plasma, but Rh-negative people do not naturally have anti-Rh antibodies. If an Rh-negative person receives Rh-positive blood, the body starts making anti-Rh antibodies, which destroy the donated red cells and stay in the body for life.

blocks.title: The true universal donor and recipient
blocks.text: O-negative is the actual universal donor, because it carries no antigen of the ABO system and no Rh antigen. AB-positive is the actual universal recipient, because it has no anti-A, anti-B or anti-Rh antibodies, so it can receive any donor's blood.
